[[#Additional roles|Additional characters]] |image2 = Noum.jpg |caption2 = ...as Noum }} '''Jason Alexander''' {{born|23|September|1959}} is a television, film, and stage actor who voiced [[Noum]] on {{s|PRO}}. Alexander is best known for his Emmy Award and Golden Globe-nominated role as George Costanza on the 1990s sitcom {{wt|Seinfeld}}. He played the role throughout all nine seasons of the show, from 1990 through 1998. Numerous ''[[Star Trek]]'' performers – including, in recurring roles, fellow ''Voyager'' guest star [[Estelle Harris]] as his overbearing mother, guest star [[Richard Herd]] as his boss with the New York Yankees, and [[Heidi Swedberg]] as his ill-fated fiancee – appeared on the show during its run, and Harris, [[Teri Hatcher]], [[Brian George]] and [[Phil Morris]] all reprised earlier roles on the series finale. == Life and career == Born '''Jay Scott Greenspan''' in Newark, New Jersey, Alexander attended that state's Livingston High School before departing before his senior year. It was while attending Livingston that he adopted Jason Alexander as his stage name. He then attended Boston University, but dropped out prior to his senior year after finding work in New York City. The university later awarded him with an honorary degree. Soon after beginning his acting career on New York stage, Alexander made his feature film debut in {{wt|The Burning (1981 film)|The Burning}} (1981, with [[Holly Hunter]]). He then acquired his first steady television work when he joined the cast of {{wt|E/R}}, from 1984 through 1985. He briefly became the star of his own series, ''Everything's Relative'', in 1987. He made infrequent appearances in film and on television throughout the 1980s, while at the same time continuing his career on the Broadway stage, including the lead role in Jerome Robbins' ''Broadway'', which garnered Alexander the 1989 Tony Award for Best Performance by a Leading Actor in a Musical. Alexander played the rotten Philip Stuckey in {{wt|Pretty Woman}} (1990). While ''Seinfeld'' was on the airwaves, Alexander had roles in such films as ''Jacob's Ladder'' (1990), {{wt|Coneheads (film)|Coneheads}} (1993, with [[Michael McKean]], [[Barry Kivel]], [[Susan Lewis]], [[Cameron]], and [[Arvo Katajisto]]), {{wt|The Paper (film)|The Paper}} (1994, co-starring [[Clint Howard]] and [[Lynne Thigpen]]), {{wt|North (1994 film)|North}} (1994, featuring [[Kathy Bates]], [[Lauren Tom]], [[Keone Young]], [[Rosalind Chao]], and [[Robert Costanzo]]), and {{wt|The Last Supper (1995 film)|The Last Supper}} (1995, with [[Ron Perlman]] and [[Amy Hill]]). He then starred in {{wt|Dunston Checks In}} (1996, featuring [[Frank Kopyc]] and [[Paula Malcomson]]) and made his feature directorial debut with the film ''For Better or Worse'', also released in 1996, in which Alexander also starred along with Robert Costanzo. And, in 1997, he starred with [[John Glover]] in ''Love! Valour! Compassion!'', based on the Terrence McNally play. Besides ''Seinfeld'', Alexander was also nominated for an Emmy Award in 1994 for his guest appearance {{wt|Dream On (TV series)|Dream On}} (1993, starring [[Chris Demetral]] and [[Wendie Malick]], with [[Iman]] and Michael McKean). Alexander was heard as the voice of Hugo the gargoyle in {{wt|The Hunchback of Notre Dame (1996 film)|The Hunchback of Notre Dame}} (1996), a role he reprised in the 2002 direct-to-video sequel and the cartoon series ''House of Mouse''. [[Tony Jay]], [[David Ogden Stiers]], and [[Frank Welker]] also voiced characters in the first film. Alexander had previously voiced bungling thief Abis Mal in Disney's direct-to-video release of ''The Return of Jafar'' and, subsequently, on the ''Aladdin'' television series. Additionally, from 1994 through 1997, Alexander voiced the title role in {{wt|Duckman}}. He supplied the voice of the evil Catbert in {{wt|Dilbert (TV series)|Dilbert}} from 1999 to 2000. In 2000, he appeared as Commander Jeffrey Pommerance in [[Jonathan Frakes]]' ''Star Trek'' spoof ''[[Star Patrol!]]''. On this project he worked with [[Michael Bailous]], [[Mel Johnson, Jr.]], [[Tom Miller]], [[Robin Morselli]], [[Brian Demonbreun]], [[Charles Rocket]], and [[Kathi Cook]]. Alexander's other film credits include {{wt|The Adventures of Rocky and Bullwinkle (film)|The Adventures of Rocky and Bullwinkle}} (2000, co-starring [[Max Grodénchik]], [[Norman Lloyd]], [[Steve Rankin]], [[Doug Jones]] and [[Whoopi Goldberg]]) and ''Shallow Hal'' (2001, with [[Bruce McGill]]). He also made appearances on such television shows as ''Friends'', {{wt|Malcolm in the Middle}}, and {{wt|Monk (TV series)|Monk}} (starring [[Ted Levine]] and [[Stanley Kamel]]) and starred in {{wt|Bob Patterson}} and {{wt|Listen Up (TV series)|Listen Up}}. An admittedly avid ''Star Trek'' fan since childhood, Alexander is such an expert on {{s|TOS}} that he passed a ''Star Trek'' knowledge test on the ''Howard Stern'' program. Alexander portrayed a parody of [[Captain]] [[James T. Kirk]] in a television special entitled ''[[Ultimate Trek: Star Trek's Greatest Moments]]''. He went on to act with the man who originated the role of Kirk, [[William Shatner]], in an episode of ''Bob Patterson'' (on which Alexander starred in the title role). He also hosted ''The Comedy Central Roast of William Shatner'' with [[Andy Dick]], [[Nichelle Nichols]] and [[George Takei]] on the dais to join in the roast, [[Clint Howard]] portraying an adult version of [[Balok]] and [[Jeri Ryan]] in the audience, and both have appeared in the Brad Paisley music videos "Celebrity" and "Online". Alexander again worked with Shatner on the computer-animated film ''Quantum Quest'', in which he and Shatner have voice-over roles. Also lending their voices to this project are fellow ''Star Trek'' alumni [[Robert Picardo]], [[Chris Pine]], and [[Brent Spiner]]. Alexander was briefly interviewed regarding his "''Star Trek'' memories" by {{STTM}}, in which he identified the first episode he remembered watching as {{e|Who Mourns for Adonais?}}, and the character he most identified with being Captain Kirk. ({{STTM|1|8|112}}) == Other ''Trek'' connections == *''Favorite Son'' (1988 mini-series, with [[Ronny Cox]], [[Richard Herd]], and [[Brian Thompson]]) *''I Don't Buy Kisses Anymore'' (1993 film, with [[Robert DoQui]]) *''Bye Bye Birdie'' (1995 television movie, with [[Vanessa Williams]]) *''The Nanny'' episode "The Tart with Heart" (1996, with [[Daniel Davis]]) *''Duckman'' episode "Where No Duckman Has Gone Before" (1997, with [[James Doohan]], [[Marina Sirtis]], and [[Leonard Nimoy]]) *''Franklin & Bash'' episode "Big Fish" (2011, with [[Malcolm McDowell]], [[Geoffrey Blake]], [[Patrick Fischler]], and [[Freda Foh Shen]]) and episode "Last Dance" (director; with [[Anne Elizabeth Ramsay]] and [[Todd Stashwick]]) *''The Orville'' with [[Seth MacFarlane]], [[Robert Picardo]], [[John Billingsley]], and [[Molly Hagan]] ==''Star Trek'' appearances== ===Appearances as Noum===

{{dis|Durango|Captain}} |image2 = Durango, 2380.png |caption2 = ...as Durango }} '''Al Rodrigo''' {{born|29|May|1960}} played [[Bernardo Calvera]] in the {{s|DS9}} [[DS9 Season 3|third season]] episodes {{e|Past Tense, Part I}} and {{e|Past Tense, Part II}}. A quarter-of-a-century later, he returned to provide the voice of [[Captain]] {{dis|Durango|Captain}} for the {{s|LD}} episodes {{e|Moist Vessel}} and {{e|The Stars At Night}}. Al Rodrigo has had supporting roles in films such as {{wt|Last Rites (1988 film)|Last Rites}} (1988, with [[Paul Dooley]]), {{wt|The Glass Shield}} (1995, with [[Bernie Casey]] and [[Lori Petty]]), {{wt|The Great White Hype}} (1996, with [[John Rhys-Davies]], [[Salli Elise Richardson]], [[Susan Gibney]], [[Albert Hall]], [[Michael Jace]] and [[Brad Blaisdell]]), {{wt|The Birdcage}} (1996, starring [[Robin Williams]]), and {{wt|House of Sand and Fog (film)|House of Sand and Fog}} (2003, starring [[Shohreh Aghdashloo]], with [[Mark Chaet]], [[Marco Rodriguez]], [[Bonita Friedericy]], [[Spencer Garrett]] and [[Michael Papajohn]]). Rodrigo has also voiced characters for film, television episodes and video games, such as ''Despicable Me'', ''Life of Pi'', ''Penguins of Madagascar'', the 2012 ''Tomb Raider'' game, ''Scooby-Doo! The Mystery Begins'', ''Mr. Peabody & Sherman'', ''Star Wars: The Clone Wars'', and ''Supernatural''. Rodrigo also guest starred in ''SeaQuest 2032'', ''The Nanny'', {{wt|Arliss (TV series)|Arliss}}, {{wt|Charmed}}, {{wt|The West Wing}}, and {{wt|NYPD Blue}}. Rodrigo also recorded ADR for {{wt|X-Men: Days of Future Past}}, {{wt|Rise of the Planet of the Apes}}, {{wt|Dawn of the Planet of the Apes}}, ''Life of Pi'', and ''Black Mass''. == External links == * {{el|alrodrigo.com|AlRodrigo.com}} – official site * {{imdb|name/nm0734989||external}} * {{wikipedia}} {{DEFAULTSORT|Rodrigo, Al}} [[de:Al Rodrigo]] [[es:Al Rodrigo]] [[Category:Performers]] [[Category:DS9 performers]] [[Category:Voice performers]] [[Category:LD performers]]
